Start line, speed and the short ones – about 40 % of all strokes.

Putting is the biggest single part of the score: a player with handicap 20 needs about 34–36 putts per round. Two skills decide almost everything: the ball has to start on the line you chose (that is the strike – the same spot on the face, the face square to the line) and it has to roll the right length. The stroke itself matters much less than in any other shot – good putters have very different strokes, but all of them start the ball on line and control the pace.

Rhythm controls the length: good putters take about the same time for a 2 m and a 15 m putt – only the stroke gets longer, not faster (Grober). A steady beat matters more for distance than any technique detail.
The face decides the start line: about 80–90 % of the start direction comes from where the face points at impact, only the rest from the path.

Tour players hole about 99 % from 0.6 m (2 ft), about 96 % from 0.9 m (3 ft), about 88 % from 1.2 m (4 ft), about 50 % from 2.4 m (8 ft) and only about 15 % from 6 m (20 ft) – long putts are about getting close, not holing.
Three-putts come mostly from the length of the first putt, not from its direction: a 10 m putt that is 1.5 m short leaves a 50/50 putt.
Dave Pelz measured that the ideal speed rolls the ball about 40–45 cm (17 inches) past the hole when it misses – the ball then holds its line near the hole and the edge “catches” it.
A hit 1 cm off the sweet spot costs about 5–10 % of the roll distance – on a 10 m putt that is up to a metre.
The two skills: start line and length

Start line means: the ball leaves the face exactly in the direction you picked. That depends on the face angle at impact and on hitting the same spot of the face every time. If you hit it off the toe, the face twists open and the ball starts right (for a right-hander) and rolls short. A gate a short distance in front of the ball shows you immediately whether the ball started on line.

Length (pace, speed) is a feel you learn by repeating it with feedback – where did the ball stop? The length comes from the length of the stroke at a steady rhythm, not from hitting harder. Most good putters swing back and through about the same length, and the stroke takes about the same time for a short and a long putt.

Start line is checked close to the ball, length at the hole.
Eyes over the ball or slightly inside it – a putting mirror shows it. Eyes outside the ball make most players aim right of the line.
Ball a little forward of centre, so the putter meets it at the low point or slightly on the way up – the ball rolls instead of hopping.
Shoulders parallel to the start line; the shoulders move the putter, the wrists stay quiet.

Aim the face first, then build the stance around it – the line on the ball can help.

A pendulum from the shoulders: the triangle of arms and shoulders moves as one piece, the hands stay passive. For most players the putter moves on a gentle arc – slightly inside going back, square at impact, slightly inside after. Do not force a straight-back-straight-through line. Through the ball the stroke accelerates gently; it should never slow down at impact.
Rule of thumb: twice the length of the backswing does not give twice the distance – learn your own scale with the ladder drill.
Rhythm: the key to length

For the length of a putt, rhythm matters most. Good putters need about the same time for a short and a long putt – a long putt is longer because the stroke is longer, not because it is faster. Whoever “adds power” on long putts or slows down on short ones loses the length.

The physicist Theodore Grober analysed videos of top players: the time of the stroke hardly changes with the length of the putt, the backstroke takes about twice as long as the forward stroke (about 2:1), and the putter meets the ball at an even speed – like a pendulum.
A metronome gives the beat: “tick” = end of the backswing, “tock” = impact. It is built in right here – no extra app needed (any metronome app works too).
Start at 72–80 beats per minute, try a few values, then keep yours – do not change it from putt to putt.
First swing to the beat without a ball, then putt short and long putts to the same beat – only the stroke gets longer.
On the course: count your beat silently during the practice stroke (“one – two”).
Same beat, longer stroke = longer putt.

Uneven lies
Ball above or below the feet, uphill and downhill – set-up and aim change.

Apart from the tee, you almost never play from a flat lie. On a slope the ground changes your posture, your balance and the flight of the ball. The good news: the rules are simple and always the same. Adapt your body to the slope, swing at about 80 % to keep your balance, and allow for the curve the slope puts on the ball. Balance matters more than any other adjustment.
Ball above the feet: the ball curves left (draw/hook) and tends to be hit heavy. Ball below the feet: the ball curves right (fade/slice) – the hardest lie for most amateurs.
Uphill the ball flies higher and shorter – often one or two clubs more. Downhill it flies lower and rolls further – often one club less.
The steeper the slope and the more loft the club has, the more the ball curves on sidehill lies.
A practice swing tells you where the club touches the ground – put the ball there.

Course management is the fastest way to lower your score – it costs no new technique. The idea is simple: every player has a shot pattern (dispersion) – no two balls land in the same spot. Aim so that the whole pattern avoids the costly trouble (out of bounds, water, deep bunkers), and accept a miss on the safe side. Most double bogeys do not come from bad swings but from bad decisions.
An average 15-handicap driver dispersion is about 50–60 m wide; a 150 m iron shot lands in an area of about 30 × 35 m.
A penalty (water, out of bounds) costs on average about 1.5–2 strokes, a fairway bunker about 0.5, the rough about 0.3 (Broadie, strokes gained).
DECADE (Scott Fawcett): tour players aim at the flag only when it is tucked away from trouble and they are close; otherwise at the centre of the green or the safe side.
A handicap 18 player who makes no double bogey plays around 85 – the “bogey plan”.

The swing: turn, sequence, tempo
Rotation instead of arms, the right sequence and a 3:1 rhythm.

A good swing is a turn around a stable centre: the body turns back, the arms swing up, and on the way down the body leads – hips, chest, arms, club, in that order. That sequence creates speed without effort. The rhythm is just as important: good players take about three times as long for the backswing as for the downswing, regardless of how fast they swing. GolfOS’s Coach module measures your six key positions; here you find the drills to change them.
Tour tempo: the backswing takes about 0.75 s, the downswing about 0.25 s – a ratio of 3:1 (John Novosel, “Tour Tempo”).
Sequence (TPI): in the downswing the hips reach their top speed first, then the chest, then the arms, then the club.
Typical turn at the top: shoulders about 90°, hips about 45° – less mobility means a shorter swing, which is fine.
The six key positions after Chris: set-up, 9 o’clock up (shaft parallel), top, 9 o’clock down, impact, finish.
Takeaway and backswing
Start “in one piece”: club, hands, arms and chest move away together.
At 9 o’clock up the shaft is parallel to the ground and to the target line, the toe points up.
The wrists hinge naturally; at the top the lead wrist is flat and the club points roughly at the target.
The weight moves into the inside of the trail foot – no sway beyond it.
Transition and downswing

The downswing starts from the ground: a small shift of pressure to the lead foot and the hips start to turn while the arms are still finishing the backswing. Then chest, arms and club follow. If the arms and shoulders start first (“from the top”), the club moves out and comes across the ball – the slice and the pull.
Impact and finish
At impact the hips are open to the target, the weight is mostly on the lead foot, the hands lead the club head.
Finish: chest to the target, nearly all weight on the lead foot, the trail foot on its toes – balanced for 3 seconds.
Tempo and rhythm

Tempo is the total time of the swing, rhythm the ratio of its parts. Your own speed can be quick (like Nick Price) or smooth (like Ernie Els) – the 3:1 ratio fits both. A metronome or a tempo app (beats “1-2-3” back, “1” down) helps to find it.
The GolfOS swing score weights rhythm with 20 % – goal 3:1.
Pulls and slices, divots pointing left.
The shoulders start the downswing; the arms are thrown out.

Difficult lies & escapes
Rough, under trees, divots, bare ground and wind – get back into play.

Every round brings a few shots from bad lies. They rarely cost one stroke – they cost two or three when you try the hero shot. The skill here is half technique (punch, knockdown, playing from rough) and half decision: the safe way back to the fairway is almost always worth more than the tiny chance of the perfect shot.
Strokes-gained data show: a ball in the trees with a free punch back to the fairway costs about 0.3–0.5 strokes; a failed hero shot into the next tree costs a whole stroke or more.
From light rough the ball often flies further (“flyer”): grass between face and ball reduces spin. From heavy rough it comes out short and low.

Wind (TrackMan): into the wind a ball loses about 0.6 % of its length per km/h, downwind it gains only about 0.3 % – headwind hurts twice as much as tailwind helps. Swing easier into the wind (“when it’s breezy, swing easy”).
Rules help: an unplayable ball costs one stroke with three options – back on the line, two club lengths sideways, or stroke and distance (Rule 19).
The punch shot under trees
Choose a 4- to 6-iron (or a hybrid): little loft keeps the ball low.
Ball back in the stance (towards the trail foot), hands clearly ahead, weight forward.
Short backswing (to hip or chest height), short finish with the hands low – hold the angle.

From the rough
Look at the lie first: sitting up (like on a tee) – normal shot, maybe a flyer; sitting down – more loft, steeper, less distance.
Grass wraps around the hosel and closes the face – grip firmer, aim a little right.
From heavy rough: wedge out to the fairway. Hybrids cut through rough better than long irons.
Divots, bare ground, wet grass
In a divot: ball slightly back, steeper swing, hands ahead – hit down, the ball comes out lower and runs.
Bare or hard ground: no extra loft, ball first, avoid the lob wedge (the bounce skips).
Wet grass: the ball flies with less spin and rolls less on landing on soft greens.
Into the wind: one or two clubs more, swing at 80 %, ball a little back – a lower ball with less spin.
Downwind: less club; the wind takes spin off the ball, so it stops less and rolls further – a higher ball is fine.
Crosswind: aim into the wind and let it bring the ball back.

Decide first: the escape rule

Ask three questions: Can I get it back into play with certainty? Where is the best place for the next shot? What does the risky shot really bring – and cost? If the gap is narrower than 2–3 m or you need a perfect curve: take the safe way. On a scorecard a bogey after a punch out is a good result.
A gap that looks like 50 % is about 10 % for an amateur.

Fairway woods & hybrids
Sweep the ball off the grass – no tops, no chunks.

Fairway woods and hybrids are the long clubs from the ground: for long par 5s, long par 3s and as a safer club off the tee. Unlike irons you do not hit down on the ball: the club sweeps along the grass and picks the ball off it, with a very shallow angle. Most amateurs top them because they try to lift the ball – or hit them fat because they swing too steep.
Hybrids are easier to hit than long irons (4- and 5-iron) for most amateurs: wider sole, lower centre of gravity, higher flight.
The attack angle with a fairway wood from the ground is close to 0° (level) – a brush of the grass, at most a thin divot.
A 3-wood from the fairway is one of the hardest clubs; a 5-wood or 7-wood flies almost as far for most amateurs and is much easier.
Ball about two ball-widths inside the lead heel (fairway wood), slightly further back for a hybrid.
Stance a little wider than shoulder width; weight 50:50.
Sole the club flat on the ground; hands level with the ball (not ahead as with irons).
The swing: sweep

Think of a wide, round swing: low and slow away from the ball, a full turn, and through the ball the club brushes the grass like a broom. Do not try to lift the ball – the loft does it. Keep the chest over the ball through impact and finish fully. With hybrids a slightly steeper, more iron-like strike is fine.
When to take a wood
Good lie in the fairway and a large target in front: yes.
Ball sitting down in the rough, a narrow green with water: rather a hybrid or a lay-up with an iron.
Off the tee on tight holes: a 3-wood or hybrid in play beats a driver in the trees.
